utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor against Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. You are still under oath. Mr. Prosecution, you are continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, perhaps just before I recommence my examination-in-chief, I understand the Tribunal was concerned to know the order of witnesses in the near future, and I would just like to let the Tribunal know of that projected order, and also for the benefit of my learned friends so that they may prepare. It is expected that Muhamed Bicic will give evidence next, Hasan Bicic after that, Ibrahim Salkic after that, and then we would propose to recall Mr. Tihic for his cross-examination. Now, I know that the Chamber has expressed a view that, if possible, all the Milan Simic victims - I use that in a -- strictly taking my guide from the indictment - but those witnesses should be dealt with all at the one time. But Mr. Tihic must be back in Bosnia for Ramadan, and it would be risky in the extreme to finish them all and not call him, because Ramadan -- he has to be back in Bosnia by the 12th of next month. So that's why we propose that order, but it will be three of the Milan Simic witnesses, so to speak. Of course, their evidence touches on other matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to hear anything from the Defence that's in accord. I'm sure that's sufficient notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It is sufficient notice. We don't have anything against this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecution can go ahead, please, with examination-in-chief. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, on the last occasion, we had dealt with the period of time you were in the SUP following your arrest, and I made it clear to you towards the end of my questioning that I was asking you only about that period of time in the SUP and before you were transferred to the TO building. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rather hard time at the time of arrest, because those were the first days when I lived through all the things that one had never dreamed of as being possible. I just don't know where they found those methods. They beat us all the time. They took turns. Each of them would come after the same thing, asking, "Where have you left your money, your jewellery, your gold?" Quite a number of times they insisted I tell them who are the sniper shooters in the Muslim part. My response was always, "What are you talking about? I have no idea about any snipers," and that in fact was the truth. I didn't know them, nor did we have any snipers, nor did we have any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the time that you were in the SUP building and before you were transferred to the TO building, you have said that you didn't have much chance to view or see other prisoners because of the fact that you were locked up alone.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, except for those that were put in the cell with me. But at one point we were so crowded one night. They brought in, I think, some 50 of them. They were from Hasici. I recognised many of them. Some were sons of my friends, friends that I used to work with in the furniture of wickerwork, in the factory of wickerwork furniture, and I heard that some had been executed, including the son of this friend of mine who was executed. It was terrible. They kept beating us, especially in the evening. They would come and they were under the influence of alcohol. They were not locals. They were all those people who were brought there, probably to do what they did. It was impossible to bear. One night they took me to this room opposite. They beat me up really badly and then they said, "Wait. We'll see what we're going to do next." And so I waited for almost an hour until the next man came, asked me, "What are you doing there?" And I said, "What am I doing? I'm waiting." And then this policeman took me back to where I was before. This other one never came back. He probably forgot about me. He had vented his fury and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, some clarification. In the beatings that were going on, any implements used, if any? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll cover those general elements now, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, I'm still confining my questions now to the period of time in the SUP building before the transfer to the TO. Firstly, can you tell us, of the people who were incarcerated with you in the SUP building, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Croats. I was the only Muslim. Later, they brought in another two or three Muslims, but then they took them away again. Also, in the morning at dawn, they took these Croats away too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: While you were in the SUP building and before being taken to the TO building, did you see incarcerated with you any obvious soldiers or military types, the people who were locked up with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the brother of Vinko Dragicevic - I think it was Dragicevic - was there. I think that was his name. He had allegedly been in Djakovo, in a military formation, and then what happened there happened. He moved to Bosnia. But he was not wearing a military uniform. He was the only one I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So I take it from your answer that none of the prisoners were dressed as soldiers or obviously soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They were all civilians. I understand now what you're asking me. They were all civilians. No one was -- there were no soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Her Honour asked -- was concerned to know whether, in the course of your being beaten and any beatings that you might have observed in the SUP building, whether weapons or instruments were used. Now, that can be anything, of course. It can be boots and so on. But can you tell us if objects were used at all in the course of your beating and other beatings you saw?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently they beat with batons. In the old days, it was called a correctional baton. I don't know what they call it now. But they also used other objects. When they would take us in that room, it was dark. There was just the candle in one corner, so one could hardly see at all. One could barely see one another. So they beat with whatever they got hold of, but especially they liked to kick. They used their fists in the face and eyes. I still have an injury in one eye. Thirty per cent of my vision has been reduced, and that was after the operation. This was done to me by someone called Cero. He punched me in the eye, together with six others that he brought with him. But it was dangerous to fall on the ground when you were being beaten, because once you fell on the ground, you never knew what happened to you, because they would kick you and then your ribs would suffer. So one didn't know what was the best position to take. They beat you to unconscious and then they'd get hold of you by the legs or by the collar and drag you along the floor and then shove you from wherever they'd brought you, and then they'd bring in the next one. It's like when they take lambs for slaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like --

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now to turn your attention to the period of time that you were in the Territorial Defence, the TO building. You've given evidence that, in fact, you were transferred there, and we all know that it was across the road from the SUP building. I'd like you to tell the Chamber what you saw when you were first taken over to the TO building.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was taken to the TO building, this one said that new ones were coming to these cells, that they needed to process them too, probably the same way they had processed me. I really had been beaten up there. I could hardly walk. They took me there, opened the iron door, and threw me inside like an object.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you see when you were thrown inside? What was in there?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside, there was, I would say, around 50 detainees. All of them had been beaten up. They were lying down. One had an eye injury. Others had his lips swollen and cracked. They were all black and blue, with their clothing torn, bloodstained. When they caught sight of me and saw what I looked like, some of them, I heard later, were glad, because they thought things were changing and that I had escaped, but I had not been guilty of anything anyway. So we were there in this room. Mr. Lukac was there too, and then these two witnesses that you mentioned a moment ago, the Bicics, and Salkic too, then [redacted], among the people I knew. I am mentioning those names. Luka Gregurevic, who was killed. Then there was a Dikan, Brandic. He was killed too in front of our very eyes. First he was hit with a pole in the head, in the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll ask you to pause there. I just want to get now some more details of the people who were in custody. I asked you before of the ethnic background of the prisoners in the SUP. Can you now comment on the ethnic background of prisoners who were in the TO with you.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, only Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again I ask you, were there any apparent soldiers or military types in custody with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was in uniform, but I noticed a couple of them who had not been hurt at all. They were sitting there. I don't know for what reason or what their role was, but they hadn't been touched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, you have told us about all these beatings in the various places. Did anyone tell you why you were being beaten or why the other civilians were beaten? That's anywhere. If not, can you tell us any reason or reasons why you were, and the others, being beaten up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They never told us why they were beating us. They just -- sometimes they would say, "You are Ustashas, you are Green Berets," and things like that. "What did you want? You wanted power in this state." I don't know what power, what they're talking about, because the authorities were already in existence, the lawful authorities, which they too had elected. They too were a part of those authorities, so what more did they want? So they beat mercilessly, and when they walked in drunk, it was so terrible. They had no criteria. They would beat until they themselves got tired of it. One day, they beat me up so badly that I could neither lie down or sit up. It was just terrible. They insulted me and my family. This was this Laki who beat me. I don't know what his name is. They called him Laki. He cursed at me, he yelled at me, he used all kinds of offensive language about my children and family. It was really horrific. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about general conditions in the TO building now, as I asked you about the general conditions in the SUP building. Can you comment on the food that you were given whilst in the TO building. You've told us about how, when you were in the SUP, they took you for lunch sometimes to the Utva factory, but now I'm talking about the TO building. What sort of food, how were you fed whilst there?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would take us from there to the Tekstilac and Utva. Those two companies were where the food was prepared. However, it was not their obligation to bring that food regularly. If they were to decide to give us lunch that day, we would have lunch. If they didn't make such a decision, we didn't have lunch. As far as conditions inside are concerned; a concrete floor. If anyone had some paper to sit on, he was lucky. It was wet. It was terrible. There were two buckets in a corner where we had to relieve ourselves. So that really, it was -- I just don't know that a normal person could do something like that because, after all, nature has made us the same, and how can one man do such a thing to another? I will not ever be able to comprehend. The torture was so awful that I haven't seen the like in films about medieval times, and I wonder myself how I managed to survive. Why all that was necessary, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about blankets at night? Did you have anything on top of you, at least? I know you didn't have anything much underneath, just a piece of paper, but what about on top? Did you have some blankets?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was nothing in the TO, no covers. If someone had something to put under his head, it was his own shoe. I spent two nights completely wet through on the concrete because this one, when he had beaten me up, he took a bucket of water and poured it over me, probably to bring me to because I had lost consciousness. And I had nothing to change into, so the clothing dried on me, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get to that beating shortly. Can you comment on the guards who were at the TO? Were they all foreigners or were some locals? When I say "foreigners," of course I mean people not from the local area.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards were all locals. And the misdeeds were carried out by outsiders, but the guards were locals. Perhaps that was our good fortune, because I must be quite frank and admit that some of them helped us. I'd rather not mention any names, because I wouldn't like them to suffer any consequences. They would bring us a glass of water or something like that, or even they would convey to us a message from our homes or would tell us about how our families were faring. So we had some luck there. But later, they learnt from the others and so they acted similarly to those others. The quickest to learn the trade was this Cera, who was taken into their ranks. This is a person -- a worthless person. He doesn't deserve to live, never mind to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was Cera a local from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a local. He was born in Bosanski Samac. His mother was not a local, but he grew up there. He went to school with my son and they were together, and just imagine what he did to his school friend's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You will provide with us a description of what he did shortly, but I'm still asking general questions about conditions in the TO. Were you ever forced to sing whilst in the TO?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the rule. As they came in through the door, they would say, "Come on, start singing." And as soon as we'd hear them coming, we would have to start singing for them to take one out and start beating him, so that his screams would not be heard. And they only sang Chetnik songs, "From Topola to Ravna Gora" and "Draza Mihajlovic." So we knew that the Yugoslav People's Army and there were Chetnik songs being sung, so nobody could understand anything any more. So we learned some songs we had never heard before in our lives. But that is what we sang all the time, all the time, until they left. And then when they'd leave, the guard would come in and say, "Stop now. Take a rest. They've gone." As I was saying, there were some guards who had some human feelings, and they just couldn't watch it. Their conscience got the better of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were singing these songs, were you forced to stand?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was compulsory. We had to stand on our feet. Even me, who had been beaten up so much. They wiped the blood off me once. Hasan Bicic and Salkic, they wiped me. And I had to sing, all beaten up like that. They would hold me under my arms. But they didn't allow me to be on the floor, because if I was on the floor, everybody would be beaten again. So they kept me standing up, and I had to sing. And he came up to me and put his ear to my mouth to hear whether I was actually singing. I was so -- everything hurt me so much. There was blood coming from my nose, from my mouth, from my ears, but still I had to keep singing. They abused me in different ways and took pleasure in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence a name, that of Dikan. Was he incarcerated in the TO with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was incarcerated in the TO. One afternoon he came. I can't say for sure whether it was Lugar or Laki. And they said, "You have the two sons. They're in the Zenga organisation. We're going to kill you first, then we're going to kill your wife and children next." And this man took up immediately an object, a wooden object - I think it was the back leg of a chair, a long piece of wood - and hit him so hard behind his neck that the man fell down and began to groan and moan, and blood shot out of his head. There was a pool of blood underneath him, and he still gave signs of life. He still moved around in this agony. Then the man took him up. There was a big pool of blood left behind him. We went completely rigid. We thought they'd take us in order, and we didn't know what to do. Apart from being able to glance at each other and give eye signals, we didn't dare talk to each other. Then the man took him by the leg, pulled him outside by the door. You have photographs of that. I've seen them. And he took out a pistol in front of the door and shot two bullets in his head, killing him. It was probably better for him to be killed rather than to have to suffer, because his skull was all hit about. And then he called another man to take him off to a warehouse on the opposite side. They took him off there. When they took him away from there, I don't know. Allegedly they threw him into the Sava River at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, the man who wielded the wooden object and hit Dikan, are you saying that it was either Lugar or Laki, one of the two, but you don't know which one?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say which one. We were afraid, you see. When they came inside, we would all have to bow our heads. We didn't dare look at them at all. If anybody were to look, to glance, and they would notice, that would be the end of him. So it was more by recognising their voices. But of course, when somebody came up to beat you individually, you would recognise that person. But I think that it was one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The comment, "You have two sons. They're in the Zenga organisation," can you make any sense of that? What ...

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Zengas. They were units, Croatian units. These Narodna Garda, or National Guard. So some of them went. They paid them. It was a professional army, and anybody who didn't have a job, who was unemployed, went to join the Zengas because they would be paid. But I don't think they followed any ideology. They didn't know where they were going, and many of them ended up as they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you about the beating that you've touched upon only briefly, and that is the attack you suffered at the hands of Cera, the man you said was a local from Bosanski Samac. First of all, is it your position -- just answer yes or no. Is it your position that beating happened whilst you were in the TO?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd like to show the witness some photographs, please. They are parts of Exhibit P14, and the photographs that I want to show are F3 -- perhaps if the whole bundle could be taken over by the usher, but the ones I immediately want to go to are F3 and F4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's get the binder that was admitted later, the one without captions, please, and that is P14A. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps if you could place on the ELMO photograph number F3 and have ready also photograph number F4, but first if we could look at F3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What does that photograph depict, Mr. Izetbegovic, just generally?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows part of the TO building. The right-hand side was where the offices were, and the higher building is the residential part which is not part of this TO building. Down at the bottom were the other offices that were used for various purposes, and part of the yard. And you can see a tap here, and they took me to that tap to slaughter me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get on to the tap in just a minute. But if you were -- where were the cells where you were being held? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On quite the opposite side, over here, opposite from this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So as you look at that photograph --

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Diametrically. It was diametrically away or diagonally away. This is where the entrance to the cells was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you would now look at photograph F4. I'm sure there won't be an objection if I suggest that shows the same courtyard, and you can see that tap area more clearly in that photograph. Are you saying that the cells where you were kept were opposite the building that you can see in the photograph which also has on it a grapevine, so that the cells were directly across from that part of the building?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, opposite that part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If one had come and stood at the door of the cell in which you were and looked out, is that what one would have seen?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could see this very well from our cell, and the door was hollow from the bullet shots. When they came into the yard, what they would do is they would shoot at the door, shoot several bullets at the door, so we knew that we shouldn't stand by the door. So that's what they would do, although some of the bullets ricocheted. And nobody was killed, although one man was grazed because he was standing nearby. So we could see through those holes often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So the way -- the reason you had a view out was the fact that people had shot holes through the door.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They shot -- there were holes in the door, and we managed to learn what was going on in the courtyard through those holes. But it was risky business. The people who dared to peep through the holes, they would give us -- make sign language and show us what was going on. They would show us by giving us sign language what was going on outside. MR. DI FAZIO: If the photo could just stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell us now of how the beating with Cera proceeded.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came, and before me they had beaten up another man. I don't remember his name now. But they had beaten him first and taken him back. Then somebody shouted out, "Izet should come out next." I just turned to glance at my friends and everything was clear to me. I went outside. Then they took me away, along this wall. They took me along this wall and told me to kneel down. Cera issued the orders and I knelt. I bowed my head down. That was the rule. You had to do that, bow your head. Then from this area here, six other men turned up, and he was standing here, next to me, over here. Then they started swearing, shouting. One of them had a red cap on, and I learnt later that that was from the State Security. Somebody must know him. He was fair. He had a red beret, the only red beret, on. All the others were wearing camouflage uniforms, masked, and they're the ones that started all this evil. And then they started beating me. They beat me and beat me until I was unconscious. Then they dragged me off to this tap here. They put my head down on this part of the concrete. My face was turned downwards to the ground. They came up behind me and asked each other, "How are we going to slaughter him? Are we going to slit the back of his neck or the front of his neck?" And I cannot find words to express how I felt at that moment. Then something happened. I don't know what happened, actually, but they kept me there for a long time, beating me and abusing me, and they kept flashing their knives and sharpening and brandishing their weapons, their knives, so to speak. And then someone from this building here shouted out something. They said, "Leave the man alone. Don't do that." And I saw many other voices round about, saying, "Don't do that. Don't do that. The man hasn't done anything. He's not to blame." And then one man took out a pistol and shot a bullet up in the air from the balcony here, towards the balcony here, and then there was silence. Everything became quiet. And there was swearing and cursing, and the man said, "We're not going to get him. We're going to get the person who is defending him." And they were two buildings adjacent to each other. I still stood there for some time, until Cera came back again and kicked me and said, "Get in there. Shove off," and I moved into that part again, into the part of the cell where I had been beforehand. And I wasn't slaughtered; I survived. Now, I can think about it in a different way now and say that maybe these were threats and they might not have done it, actually, carried out the threat, but whatever the case, I wouldn't wish this to happen to anybody, even my worst enemy. I wouldn't wish this fate upon even my worst enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you receive any particular injuries on this occasion? By that, I mean other than bruises and the like.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: From the very first moment they beat me, and later on when they beat me, I couldn't know which injury was from which actual beating, because they would be repeated; the injuries would be repeated. I couldn't count how many broken ribs I had. My face was all bashed in, with the same injuries occurring. I couldn't see out of one of my eyes for some time. Up until 1993, until I had an operation in Zagreb, I was unable to see out of one eye. And all the rest of it. My hands were all bashed in, I forgot to say. They did this in the SUP. They would place my hands on the table and then they would beat me on the hands, and the man that did this said, "You won't be able to sign anything ever again. You won't need the use of your hands any more." And it was all swollen and inflamed, terrible. And I was lucky to find a little bit of water somewhere and put my hands in the water to ease the swelling and inflammation. Finally, when I was exchanged, I learnt that I actually had nine broken ribs, I had no teeth left in my head, I had my damaged eye, completely damaged. My sight has been impaired 70 per cent. I can only see 30 per cent, whereas I never had to wear glasses before. I do now. I was never ill in my life, except a fracture perhaps, but nothing serious. I was never, ever ill in my life. And the number of blows to my head, I can't even count them. They would especially target my head and keep hitting me on the head with the batons they had, so that even today I feel frequent pain, particularly when the weather changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned injuries to your hands. Do you still have -- I'll rephrase my question. Do you have full movement in your hands and fingers?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything has been reduced. I can't stretch any of my fingers normally. Look, like this. That's the best I can do, because a lot of them -- there were a lot of fractures. My little finger, I can't straighten that at all, or the middle finger either. Each finger -- the function of each finger has been impaired and deformed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Izetbegovic. We didn't quite see your hand. Can you put it up and do that again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it's like. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Hold them up. Perhaps you can show them on the ELMO as well. Perhaps one at a time. We can get a good view there. One at a time, and turn them over, if you can. Thank you. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: And I've finished with the photograph, that particular photograph. Perhaps if the bundle could just remain at the ELMO machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. di Fazio, could you describe what we saw there. MR. DI FAZIO: Is Your Honour referring to the hands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, for the purposes of the transcript, Mr. Izetbegovic demonstrated both of his hands on the ELMO. One could see one of the little fingers on his hand -- on his right hand completely bent back, and the middle finger on one of the hands, I'm not sure which, bent sideways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber has observed deformed fingers. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you were being beaten by Cera in the courtyard of the TO building, were you screaming out or crying out?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what it's like when it hurts. I can't actually remember how much I screamed, but others say -- whether I screamed, but other people said that I screamed and groaned every time they hit me. That's what the others told me that I met from the building. They said, "How could you take it all? We thought that they had killed you." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You described having to -- spending two nights in the TO building drenched or wet. When did you spend those two nights wet through in relation to this beating by Cera, before or after?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after that. Before the others went to Brcko. Cera also beat me afterwards, when the others had gone off to Brcko. And that night I stayed and three others stayed with me, me and three others, whereas the rest went to Brcko. And they told us that we were being kept back and that they would execute us, that that's why they had left us behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If I could show one more photograph and it's the last one for the time being, and that's photograph F1 of the exhibit. F1, the first photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has been altered. I assume that this is the cell we were locked up in, but this door seems to be new. It's not the broken-down door that I remember, or they have altered it in some way, because you can see this building and that was right opposite where we were. But they seem to have altered it. You can see that they have built in a new door and put some mortar on it. But I assume that that's where we were locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at the photograph carefully, is part of the grapevine that you can see in the other photographs that I showed you, F3 and F4, is that partly visible through the door, in the distance?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it. Here it is. That's the grapevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look onto the ground near where the policeman or soldier is standing. You see what appears to be a square with a handle on it on the ground, like a drain cover. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where it was, in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it saved us. The drain saved us once, the drain cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when they would beat us, then underneath -- they beat us with chains as well as blunt objects, iron blunt objects. And then one morning, they would take us out there to relieve ourselves if we wanted to, to do our physiological -- see to our physiological needs, because the WC was opposite. And then we'd go one by one. We'd go outside. One of us would go off and then come back, one by one. And during that time, one -- they used chains to chain off the area. Once they lifted the manhole or drain cover and threw the -- lifted the lid and threw the chain inside, and none of the guards saw us -- saw this chain being thrown away. We thought it would be easier to take blows with blunt objects rather than being beaten with a chain. So we threw the chain away down the drain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, and I can tell the usher that I've finished now with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we leave that section, I'd like to ask the witness for clarification. Was it a metal chain? And regardless of the answer, was that -- did you see that chain being used to beat anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were metal chains, and I saw them being used. I think that it was used against the Bicics too. But their nephew, nicknamed Roma, hid the chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You mentioned that prisoners were taken to Brcko. I want to now ask you about that occasion. Were you in the TO building at the time that they were transferred to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The truck turned -- a truck turned up in the evening hours, towards evening, and the guards came with a list. And they called the names out from the list and put the men one by one into the truck. Luka Gregurevic, myself, we stayed on, and two others, the father the Vinko Dragicevic, and the other person that stayed behind was Dr. Kedacic. That's right. He stayed. We stayed behind. And when we asked why, why we weren't on the list - I didn't ask but others asked - they said, "You'll stay behind because you're going to be executed, shot." The others boarded the truck and left in an unknown direction. Later on, we heard that they had in fact gone to Brcko, whereas they transferred us that night to the police station, up there to the cells where I had come from originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you remain back in the SUP building, in the cells where you had come from originally?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but it could have been a day or two. Until I had to go for the making of that infamous film by Mr. Zaric, which is an absolute lie, a fabrication, exactly in the way in which things were done in the former Yugoslavia, the false trials and all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So your position is that that interview took place after the men had been transferred to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they were brought for that filming of that cassette nevertheless. They were brought there. I saw them there. When I was taken inside, they were leaving. So I suppose they took them back to Brcko again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get on to that tape shortly. What was -- what ethnic background was Dr. Kedacic?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat from Vinkovci, on duty in Bosanski Samac. He was employed in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He was a doctor, was he?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a doctor, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: A medical doctor, a physician?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a physician, a medical doctor. He may have been a specialist as well, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had he been beaten?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was beaten quite a bit too. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'd like now to show the film "Genocide in Bosanski Samac." The exhibit number I don't have at the top of my -- off the top of my head. I'd just ask for it to be identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it P6? I hear it's P6. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: P6. Thank you. If that could be arranged now to be shown. I believe transcripts have already been provided to the Court. If that could be shown. I believe that transcripts have already been provided to the Court, and I have arranged with the gentleman in the technical room to take us to the relevant portions rather than play it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- the whole of the tape in its entirety. And I think, for the record, it should be P16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's P16. MR. DI FAZIO: P16 rather than P6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm corrected. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please be given a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the interpreters are asking for transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: That should have been provided, I believe. It was -- I don't propose to refer to the content of the interview itself. I'm merely going to ask the witness to identify the various portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The various places. MR. DI FAZIO: The various places, those places that are depicted in the interview itself, so we won't need the transcript today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: So I would ask that the exhibit could be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, we're going to play a tape, and I would like you to watch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Izetbegovic, do you recognise that gentleman that you can now see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. MR. DI FAZIO: If we could now just proceed to 11:20 on the tape, on the video cassette, on the counter, at the point 11 minutes and 20 seconds, please, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: And if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the gentleman currently shown? MR. DI FAZIO: Could we just stop there, please. Just rewind it back again for Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is Mr. Zaric and the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at Mr. Zaric's right -- sorry, left arm. Do you see a white object just underneath the microphone?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the white ribbon that they tied. I don't know why. I don't know what the reason was. Probably to recognise one another, to know who was a member of the 4th Detachment. I don't know. They know best what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. You've described earlier in your evidence last week that members of the 4th Detachment had white ribbons. Can you tell us if they were wearing the sort of white ribbon that you can see there on Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just like that, a piece of white rag tied to the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like that. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we now proceed to the point 13:06 on the tape counter.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Pause there, please. Could we just go back and pause where we can see the gentleman in the tan jacket.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, who is that?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a journalist from Novi Sad who interviewed us, who was probably the leader of the team, together with Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm more interested in the gentleman on the right.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Look at your hand.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know very well what it looked like. Could the technicians please enlarge the hand, if possible, focus in on the hand, zoom in on the hand? I have this tape at home, so I think it's possible technically. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I don't think it is, but we'll be able to see the hand in closer detail, if we could just go back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. di Fazio. I wonder whether you could also zero in, if it's possible, on the witness's face, because it's my understanding a few moments ago, I believe, that Mr. Izetbegovic had mentioned that he didn't wear glasses until recently, or until after these events, and it could be my eyesight, but I seem to see him wearing glasses in this video. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I don't recall him saying that, but there is a shot that will show precisely what Your Honour is concerned about, and I'll ask him about the question of the glasses as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks. If we could just go back to the film now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Now, just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Her Honour asked if you were wearing glasses there. Now, it's not very clear in that one. We'll get to a clearer photo. But can you see if you're wearing spectacles there?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have glasses there. They gave them to me. And when you see the rest of the film, you will see that most people have glasses, because those who were really badly beaten were given glasses. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Could we just continue now the film at normal speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you see my hand. They can wind back a little bit to show that hand. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we just rewind briefly now to the point at which you can see Mr. Izetbegovic. If we could just rewind briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I request for my hand and head to be shown close up. I think it is very important. MR. DI FAZIO: Could the film be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: And could it be rewound briefly to the point at which we were looking at before, around 13:06, 13:16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Now, if we could just pause it there, please. If we could just go back briefly, thank you, and just pause it to where we can see the two men, the interviewer and Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were supplied with spectacles or glasses. We'll see precisely what sort of glasses later, I think. Were you a wearer of glasses before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never wore any dioptric glasses, except for sunglasses sometimes, like all other people. The fact that I look so nicely dressed here, they sent somebody to our homes to find our suits. We had a bath, we had a shave, we got dressed for the filming that day, to look normal. Otherwise, we were all bloodstained and look awful in the clothes we wore normally. All this was rigged. Nothing was real.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you -- just leaving it, holding it there, you mentioned that it was TV Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was the interviewer apparently Serbian, of Serbian origin or background?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that he came from Novi Sad, because they have a dialect of their own, a special way of speaking, so I don't really know what his ethnicity was. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Could we now fast forward the film to the point 15:30 on the counter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The gentleman with that astonishing hairdo, do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do very well. Ramusovic, also known as Tota, a man who was turned back from his regular military service. I know him rather well because he was my next-door neighbour. He was turned back from the army. He didn't complete his military service as being immature. And he turned out to be one of the reliable, more reliable members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we now fast forward it to the point 24:40 on the counter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise that gentleman also wearing sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Omer Nalic, technical director of the Elektrodistribucija company. He never wore glasses, but those are sunglasses. We had several pairs of spectacles on the table, and this gentleman taking the film knew what they needed among props. And they would give glasses to us to try, and those that they thought fitted business, that is, that covered our bruises best, were left on us. And never for a moment -- when Mr. Zaric was talking, he saw that we were beaten up, and never for a moment did he ask us, "What is that? Why? How did you get those bruises?" Why did he film us? How can he justify that? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was Omer Nalic incarcerated in the TO building when the group of 50 men or so were there, whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was brought when I was transferred to the TO. Until then, he was doing his normal duties in the power supply system, because everyone went to work. And that is where they picked him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we now proceed to the point 25:30 on the counter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you recognise that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Safet Hadzialijagic, also known as Coner. He was head of the water supply system in Bosanski Samac. That is where I was arrested, in his apartment, in front of my daughter's. I crossed over to him in my slippers, and that is where they found me. He went occasionally to examine the water supply system until they finally took over. And I was in the SUP, in the cell, and then I saw him being brought in and thrown into another cell, so that there wasn't enough time for him to be beaten so badly as to need glasses. His face was clean, unhurt, unbruised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. This gentleman's surname, Safet what?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hadzialijagic, and also known as Coner. Hadzialijagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: And if we can proceed now to the point 29:09 on the counter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who is that man?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is attorney Sulejman Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If we could now proceed to 33:10. And for the assistance of the technical room, the point -- the objects that I'm looking at this point are the depiction of some houses of worship. I believe they're at 33:10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If we could just pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What's that place?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Bosanski Samac. MR. DI FAZIO: And could we just continue the film now at normal pace.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What's that building there with the stripes?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Orthodox church or place of worship, across the way from the Catholic church. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If we could proceed again.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what's that building that we could see depicted there?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Muslim place of worship, or mosque. MR. DI FAZIO: If we could now proceed to the point 35:20 on the counter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: While we're getting there to 35:20, can I ask you, Mr. Izetbegovic, do you know if the mosque and the Catholic church are still standing in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they're not standing. They were both destroyed. There's not a stone left of the Muslim mosque to know that that is where it stood. As for the Catholic church, they have done some repairs. I went there on my own by car. I passed through Samac. I didn't even stop at my own house, because I had had enough of everything. I got in the car, drove around, and went back. I feel even worse than before I went. It doesn't look like the town it used to be. I just can't understand how those people intend to live if they go on in that way. The town will disappear. I simply don't know why they needed to destroyed those places of worship. By this very act they demonstrated that they didn't wish to have members of the other ethnic group in their vicinity. We used to visit one another. We used to go to those places of worship. I attended the midnight service, as I said once to a question from the attorneys. We looked forward to those events. There was absolutely no reason to do something like this. It's such a shame. These were the only historical documents testifying to the way people used to live. How will the future generations see that we existed there, that we lived there? They have destroyed all traces of that. I just don't know why, what the gentlemen who did that wanted to achieve. I don't wish to generalise. I do not wish to say in that Tribunal that this was done by the people. I still think it was done by individuals who were sick in the head and led by sick ideologies. And that is why this Tribunal was formed, to try those sick minds and not to put a whole nation on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Izetbegovic. Now, look at the film. MR. DI FAZIO: If the film could just be played at normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you can see your hand there. Was it swollen? MR. DI FAZIO: Just pause there. Perhaps if we continue just a bit further with the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you see any black around your eyes?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My eyes were swollen. Everything was black. I don't know how these gentlemen who were making this film - I don't wish to mention any names - how they weren't ashamed to film me looking the way I did without asking me, "What happened to your eyes?" To beat me first and then to film me. I really don't know whether they have any honour or any feeling or any sense in them, or were they so imbued with this idea that if people didn't think the way they thought, then -- if they didn't think like the police, like the UDBA, thought in the old days, then they were not fit to live there. That is how they acted, anyway. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we just continue the film at normal speed.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. It's 11.00. If Your Honours please, would that be an appropriate point to adjourn for the morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have our break now, and we will continue at 1130 hours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't want to show the video to the witness any more, but I do want to refer him to the content of it, and the simplest way of doing it, I think, is by asking to be produced to the witness the transcripts, or rather, the B/C/S transcript of the video. The interpreters' booth has, I've been assured, both English and B/C/S versions, and the Court, the Chamber, should have its own copies, of course, of the transcript. So can the witness please be provided with P16A/1 ter, which is the transcript of the video that we've just been looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, I believe that the transcript of the B/C/S has now been given to you. I don't need to use the ELMO for purposes of this portion of the examination-in-chief. Mr. Izetbegovic, you were shown twice on that tape. I'm interested in the second occasion in which you appeared. And on the English version, the English translation of the transcript, which is at page 13, if Your Honours please, is at the very end of the tape. So I suggest that you go to the end of the B/C/S version, and you will see yourself identified. In fact, I believe it's also on page 13 that you can see the transcript begin. I'd ask you just to read from the point where the journalist commences, "All the people who had agreed to appear on television and who talked to us," and would you just read, read the transcript to yourself to the bottom of that page, all of the next page, and to the end of the transcript on page 15. MR. DI FAZIO: For the assistance of the usher, I believe it's on page 13 of the B/C/S version, and I think the word "novinar," n-o-v-i-n-a-r, is "journalist." It's from that portion until the end of the portion that I'm interested in. Can you just read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to try and answer with respect to the first question put to me by the journalist, although I think that the question itself has been posed in such a way that I don't really know what to say. They said -- when they say that I'm guilty, that I was to blame, then I think that we should ask them whether they were voluntary witnesses or not. We were afraid of everything. If they said, "Did you kill a man?" I might have said yes, just to stop them from beating me, because everything under duress, under threat, coercion. I don't know what other witnesses will say, but I too was under the effects of this fear. I spoke as frankly as I dared. I didn't wish to sidestep any responsibility, because I was one of the leaders of the people that I lived with, like everybody else. But I didn't have the consciousness of having done any harm to anybody. I did not arm [as interpreted] anybody. There was not a single bullet shot fired. This had nothing to do with Alija. What I have been accused of -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What I'll do is I'll assist you, Mr. Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll assist you, Mr. Izetbegovic, by asking you questions and directing you to certain portions of the transcript, okay? Now, firstly, the initial question of the --

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- of the portion of the transcript that I've directed your attention to is a journalist speaking, who says, "All the people who have agreed to appear on television blame you." Now, before you went into this interview, had you been informed or told who the people were and what they had said?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell me who the people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I could ask Mr. Izetbegovic a question. The other people who appeared on the programme, were they brought to the TV station with you in the same vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, thus far I've only dealt with the actual interview itself, the content of it. I will, at the conclusion of this, ask some questions about the surrounding circumstances. So I'll cover that aspect later. I've perhaps approached it the wrong way around, but I will cover the circumstances under which the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because I could see from the very beginning, when you introduced the transcript, that you're trying to show what were the circumstances -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- and were the people, especially the witness himself, was he still in custody. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. I'll attend to all of those matters once I've dealt with the actual content of the interview itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, you say -- a journalist asked you about your name being on the list of SDA military headquarters, and you replied that you had a security commission but it had too much authority and it was your biggest mistake. First of all, was that a correct reflection of your own views; and secondly, was it correct in fact that the security commission had too much, too much authority and power?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept at all the film, the tape that was filmed and the conversation with the journalist as something normal, because normal conditions simply did not exist. When you have in front of the door armed guards with bayonets and inside where you're sitting you have people wearing uniforms, asking you, then I ask you now, how would anybody behave were they in my place? So I had to say something and accept something and take responsibility for something, as far as I dared, and to make it a text that would be acceptable to all parties. So I said I do not wish to say that I am not entirely to blame. Perhaps there was some blame that I did not prevent the people from being arrested. That's where I saw my blame. As for arms and weapons, everybody was armed. Everybody could buy weapons for themselves. And I said that in a previous contact with you. So that I still feel guilty for not putting this under control and having the weapons surrendered, handed in, as far as I was able.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the interviews were not normal. They were not conducted under normal circumstances. They all said what the others wanted to hear. I'm not even saying that they were actually coerced, but they went in one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the course of this interview, and you can see it in the transcript that I've directed your attention to, you discuss a joint HDZ-SDA staff for Bosanski Samac, that you were against it, the formation of such a staff, and that, for you, the formation of such a staff was a declaration of war. Now, do you see that in the transcript? Now, all I want to know is does that accurately reflect reality?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting where we tried to do something along those lines. I prevented it at the outset. I didn't allow it. One side pulled in their direction, but it is also true that the other side pulled in the other direction. And we were a party which somehow was - what shall I say - was the smallest as regards population and numbers, and I prevented this. I didn't allow it. And I did say that this would be a declaration, and we know a declaration of war to whom. If the two of us pooled together, then it would be against the third party. So I wasn't in favour of that variant, because I thought that this arming and weapons and everything else, that it would all calm down, that this was just a burgeoning of one particular moment by people who had come in who knows where from. So I too probably wasn't fully conscious of what it would all lead to. But it was difficult. That's how things stood. And I mixed up the meeting and said that the SDA would not -- never enter into a coalition with anyone, but we wanted to agree. We didn't want to have a classical type of coalition. We rejected that straight away at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the end of the transcript, you were asked by the interviewer whether Muslims and Serbs could find a common language because of a lack of historical differences, and you reply, and in your reply you stress that your family comes from Belgrade, that you're the only Izetbegovic family from Belgrade. What was the purpose of referring to that? The reference to Belgrade, I mean.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of mentioning that was that I was asked a very difficult question by the journalist, and that was: "Why do you Muslims hate the Serbs?" That was his question. And I tried to answer, first of all, by saying that I was going to answer in a way that wasn't usual but if they would believe me. And Mr. Zaric was present on the occasion. And I indicated a banal point. I was conscious of the fact that arrests were being made and that they were burgeoning, and now I kept thinking about what would happen to the people. Where were they taking the people off to? And I wanted to try and calm this down, to say that not everything was like that. Why should the Muslims hate the Serbs, as we had lived so well together? There weren't any instances of conflict on the whole of the municipality between Serbs and Muslims or with the Croats, or between the Croats and Serbs either. But at that -- during those times, that's what happened. And so I answered. I told him how this came about, and what I said was that I had played a lot of football in my life and that I was well acquainted with football. I was an active fan and an active member of the Bosanski Samac football club. And, "When you say and maintain that the Muslims hate the Serbs, then answer my question and tell me why Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. everybody from Bosanski Samac, all the fans, are in favour of the Partizan club and the Red Star, Crvena Zvezda club? And if they hated them, they wouldn't rally for them." And they laughed at this. And the people who are still in Samac today said, "Well, you couldn't think of anything to talk about except those stupid little things." They're not stupid things. That was a last attempt, a final attempt to have the people doing this realise that that wasn't the reason and that they would say, "If that is like that, just leave the people alone. It's not true that they hate them." But I didn't succeed in doing what I wanted to achieve. They carried on doing what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: I've finished with the transcript, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Izetbegovic, you've told us about the content of the interview, and we've seen parts of the interview. I now want to ask you about the circumstances of the interview. You've said that it occurred after the men were taken to Brcko. Do I understand you correctly, therefore, to be saying that it occurred whilst you were in custody but in the TO -- but in, sorry, the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was down there in the SUP building, and that's where they took me, processed me, cleaned me up, cleaned me up and took me to be filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did they clean you up? Where were you taken? Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, or rather, the evening before, Todorovic turned up and took me out of the cell. He took me outside, in front of the door. And it was dusk. It was getting dark, but you could still recognise the faces of people who were there. And he said, "Some relatives have come to see you. Come out and see them." I didn't know what this was all about, and I saw a whole television crew standing at the door. And Todorovic said, "Now do you believe that he's there?" They were asked to come and conduct that interview and they took me back to the cell. Then, in the morning, a policeman came and said, "Come on. You're going --" First of all, they asked me whether I had anybody at home who could bring me a change of clothing. I said, "Yes, my daughter, but she is not at home. She is married and lives with her in-laws." And then they said, "Can we go and fetch her for her to find you a change of clothing so that you can change?" And I said, "Well, if you manage to find her, you can." They didn't say I was actually going to be filmed. They said, "You're going to be exchanged." They said, "You're going to be exchanged, so it would be a good idea for you to get cleaned up and changed a bit," and I waited for a little while for them to go to my home and bring these things back. In the meantime, a man came to see me, and I can say of that man that he was well disposed towards me. He helped. He helped the prisoners. I don't wish to state his name, but he did have a significant role in all of this. I can't say that he did any bad things in Samac. I don't know if he did elsewhere. But he said, "Here's a carton of cigarettes, a pack of cigarettes. I've brought this to you now, but I don't dare do it again. I don't know if I'll ever see you again, in fact." And I whispered to him, "It seems that I'm going to be exchanged today," and his answer was, "Oh, I don't think you're right in the head. Who is going to exchange you for whom? They don't dare do that. They have to treat you first and then when you have recovered, they can exchange you." And he left and I never saw the man again. Then the policeman came to fetch me, and my daughter had come as well, bringing me a change of clothes, underwear and a suit. And when she saw me, well, it was a very difficult moment. It was difficult for her and it was difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you able to bathe, shave?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They put me in a Golf car. There were two policemen with me. And they took me to the Separacija, by the bricklaying factory. They took me over there to the factory bathrooms to shave and wash, have a shower, and they stood guard throughout that time while I was washing and shaving. So that that's what I did. I finished cleaning up, I changed my clothes, and they took me back to the SUP building. They didn't take me back to the cell. They put me in one of the offices on the upper floor, and that's where I waited. I didn't know what was going to happen. Then at one point they came to fetch me again and took me to Omer Nalic's office and I saw Simo Zaric there, and the journalists with their cameras were there and everything had been prepared. That was quite clear. And there were a lot of these sunglasses laid out on the table, five or six different pairs of sunglasses, and I had to take some glasses and the filming began. Zaric didn't ask me anything. It was just the journalist that put the questions to me. But when I got the entire tape -- and I can say that I got it from Belgrade, and there are people there too whose conscience is clear and who are good and well-intentioned people, and they sent me that. And I have a lot of other things from Belgrade sent to me too, what the papers wrote about me as well. And that's where the filming of that tape started. When I saw the tape later on and saw what Mr. Zaric -- well, I hope he won't take this amiss, but he is a professionally deformed person. He never did anything else in his life but police jobs. He was a director for a very short time, and his retirement was what he took the hardest, because he thought that it was only up to him to think about the fate of Yugoslavia. He thought that everybody was of less value when it came to Yugoslavia's fate. That's what I think about him, and I think that many people would agree with me. So it was this professional deformation on his part which is costing the people, and all of us; it has cost all of us a great deal. And everything that he showed on the tape, the children who were armed, those are all lies. In the entire region, there is no institution for retarded children. Where he found that, where he got that from, I don't know. And Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic mentioned some three days of fighting when they moved from one river bank to another. There was no fighting - let me make that clear - except when they started shooting to make the people frightened when they came into Samac. Nobody offered any resistance. There was no fighting whatsoever, and it is in their fear that they shot while they were walking along the streets to instill fear in the people. That's what happened. And that's what it was like right to the end of the tape. The whole tape was filmed as somebody wanted it to be filmed, because they probably expected to become a general at the end of it all. So I can't accept any of the details on the tape as being actually correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned some of the people who were present. We can see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We can see from the tape itself that the interviewer was obviously there, Mr. Simo Zaric was there, you were there. At the time of your interview, at the time that you were speaking, was Simo Zaric present?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was. He was sitting opposite me, I think. Yes, yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was Stevan Todorovic ever around?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he too was sitting at his desk, and there were the cameramen, one or two of them. You see, it's hard to remember. When you're in such a situation, one is full of fear. There was fear, above all else. I am not ashamed to say that I was scared, and perhaps I didn't really register all the people who were present. I was looking at the journalist most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that a number of other people were interviewed for the purposes of the same programme: Omer Nalic, Sulejman Tihic, and so on. On the occasion that you were interviewed, did you have a chance to see them being filmed or photographed, or even just speak to them, prior to or after their filming?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them at all. It was only on tape that I realised that they were filmed too, but this was later, when I left the camp. And I learnt also later what their opinion was about all those things, how the film was made and everything. They also said more or less what I am saying. We were fearful, and when one is afraid, one says things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, do you need that evidence? The people can come and say so on their own. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just try and confine your answers to my questions, if you can, Mr. Izetbegovic, and if I need more information, then rest assured that I'll ask you to expand upon a particular point. How long did the filming take, obviously the portion that you're involved in?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me to last a long time. I assume I must have spent at least an hour there, because I know I smoked quite a number of cigarettes. They gave me these cigarettes. So I can't tell you exactly. I didn't have a watch on, so I don't know. Under such circumstances, it seems like eternity, but I think it was about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've commented already on the content of the interview. Was there any discussion prior to the interview of what the questions were to be?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not at all. When I was taken inside, it was only then that I realised what was going on and what I was expected to do. This journalist said to me, "You are going to give an interview. Do you agree?" And I said, "Yes. What I know, I'll tell you; what I don't know, I don't know." I didn't know what he was going to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following the interview, were you taken downstairs, back to your cell?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they took me back to the cell and nothing came of the exchange. It was all a lie. I was misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you eventually transferred away from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of days later, they put Dr. Kedacic, myself, and Dragicevic in a police Golf car, and two policemen drove us. We were handcuffed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll get on to that in a moment, but before I leave the topic of your period of time in Bosanski Samac, I want to ask you about the presence of or lack of the defendants in and around the SUP building. Now, you have told us in some detail of encounters that you had with Mr. Simo Zaric. Whilst you were in Bosanski Samac and in prison, either in the SUP or in the TO, did you see any of the other defendants around the buildings?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, roughly. I said I saw once in the corridor -- I was being taken upstairs - I don't know what the reason was - and there was Dr. Simic in the corridor. He must have seen me. He couldn't not have seen me. And then I also saw Simo Zaric, since the door is thin and you can hear in the corridor what is being said inside, and I could hear his voice quite a number of times in the corridor. And I could recognise almost all of them by their voices. And I also saw -- when they would take us to lunch, when we were being boarded onto trucks, then we would cast a glance around, and I would then see Simo Zaric. And I also saw Simo Zaric -- you see, we forgot that, but it's very important and I do apologise for having to go back again to the TO. I saw him there under far-from-pleasant -- in a far-from-pleasant encounter. I didn't expect that of him or of Dr. Simic. If I can tell you about that now. If that is acceptable, I could tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you just tell us about the time you described as a far-from-pleasant encounter when you saw Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had really had enough of this torture and these beatings, I appealed to a policeman, who was the son of a friend of mine, to find Simo Zaric, for him to come and see what we looked like and for us to ask him something.
