He did as I asked, and he went and told us Simo would come, but we didn't know when. And we waited for him. And he came in the afternoon in a camouflage uniform, of course. As soon as he came through the door, he said to us, "Don't let anyone ask me anything, but let me say this to you: These men who beat and tortured you, they have left today. From this moment on, I am taking over full command of the town. You will all be processed, and who is guilty will be held responsible. Who is not guilty will, of course, be released." And we rejoiced, because this would be the first night that we would not be beaten. That was the first reason. And he left, because he said no one may ask him anything. In the evening, around 9.00, these men came, and that was the worst beating we had, because, in fact, they had never left. I don't know what Mr. Zaric intended. If he had let us speak up -- he must have seen how we looked. Fifty per cent of the people were people who socialised with him, who were friends. And surely in those 15, 20, or 30 years, he could have known who these people were, that they hadn't deserved that. He never moved a finger. He just left. And that evening, we were really badly beaten up. And they continued their daily routine. So this was just a minor incident -- an incident that I had forgotten. We can now resume where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for letting me mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, before I forget the point that I have in my mind, this incident when the witness says Mr. Simo Zaric met them and told them no more beatings and the people had left, when was it; in April, May? In relation to the period when he was in custody and the period up to the time he was released, was it in May, at the beginning, in the middle, or towards the end? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Perhaps I can ask the witness this. That might be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This occasion when Simo Zaric came along and told you he had taken over control of the town and you were going to be processed and so on, when did that occur in relation to the transfer of the men out of the TO to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This occurred before the people were transferred to Brcko. I think it was immediately after the murder of Dikan. Somewhere there. But it did occur. Please don't ask me to be quite specific about it, because I can't remember the date exactly. But it happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- exactly in the way I've told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. So you place it sometime between the murder of Dikan and the transfer of the majority of men to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, let's go -- now, we dealt with Mr. Zaric. Now let's go back to Mr. Blagoje Simic. You told us that you saw him in the SUP, and you've also given evidence that you saw him on occasions at the Utva when you were having lunch. I'm interested in the occasions at the SUP. How was he dressed when you saw him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you see him on only one occasion or more than one occasion at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was only on that one occasion. Maybe twice. I'm not quite certain about the second occasion. I wasn't in a normal state. You know, when you get a good hiding, you can't remember so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now let's turn our attention, please, to your transfer away from Bosanski Samac. You started telling us that you were taken to Pelagicevo in a car. Who went with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two policemen. I knew them before, but I'm afraid I've forgotten their names now. I can't remember their names. But I knew both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the three of us on the back seat, Dr. Kedacic, Dragicevic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pelagicevo, we stopped in front of the cultural centre or the school, whatever it was. I think it was the school. No, no. It was the cooperative centre. And then they said, "Don't you try anything." They locked us up in the car, and we waited. At one point in time, two of them came out and a commander of theirs, and I could see that they were quarrelling. And we looked at one another, thinking, What next? And only when they approached the car we could hear them saying, "I will not take out a firing squad unless I have at least ten people. I will not take out a firing squad for three." We went -- we were petrified. We looked at one another, and then Dr. Kedacic said, "This really is the end." Believe me, we said to one another, "Forgive me for everything." We consoled one another. We were really terrified. So I really don't know what my thoughts were at that moment. Then they moved away from the car, went inside. They continued quarrelling. I kept looking around at the little -- at the thickets where they would take us, and I thought to myself where my bones will lie and no one will know where they are. And then after some time, they did take out a firing squad. Ten men under arms, in camouflage uniforms, came out, and they went in the direction of the helicopter which had previously landed. When we had arrived, it was already there. It was a military helicopter. And we thought to ourselves they would board us on the helicopter and then take us someplace, into a wood somewhere far, where no one would be able to find us. They lined up, and then -- we were still in the car. We were still waiting. A small vehicle came up carrying a coffin with a dead man inside. They took out the coffin. Then they performed the tribute of -- firing tribute. Then we realised that this was all it was about. Then they boarded the coffin after the salute, and they came back for us, put us in the helicopter. One of them fired a shot with a Kalashnikov. I still have the scars from the handcuffs. Nobody took off those handcuffs. We were tied one next to the other, and we boarded the helicopter in that way. And when we got inside, I saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I shouldn't have interrupted you. What did you see when you got inside?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on the coffin the surname Zurovac and the birth. It was my good friend's son, Raka Zurovac, in Orasje, who was killed on the front line. He was dressed. As we were neighbours, next-door neighbours. We celebrated when he was born. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you taken anywhere in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The helicopter started. There were several men under arms with us inside. Again we thought they were -- would throw us out of the helicopter someplace. Never for a moment did I think that they were taking us for some good reason, for something positive. All that we had in mind was that they were going to execute us. Suddenly the helicopter landed. Again we didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. Were you joined by anyone?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The door opened and I saw Mr. Tihic come in, also Dragan Lukac, the vet Anto, Franjo Barukcic. He's no longer alive. A policeman who used to be in active duty before, his name was Sejo. I can't remember his surname. Then also -- there were nine of us in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the helicopter take off and depart for somewhere?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it took off again, and we travelled for some time. Where we had landed was in Bijeljina. After that, we were in the air for some time. We again didn't know where we were going, and then it landed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where did you land?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we didn't know where we were. Later, we learnt that we were at Batajnica, near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like you to tell us about conditions at Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we got off the helicopter, the torture started again. The captain, the army captain, air force captain - he was wearing a blue uniform - ordered us to lie down, face down, quickly. Then he started in his own -- the way that army was wont to do. He lectured us: "It's a shame to execute you. Bullets are expensive. You're not worth a phennig." And then: "We'll get rid of you in another way." Then the order came to get up. A small van came. We boarded it. We travelled for some time, until we came to the area in which we were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. incarcerated. So the van got to in front of the door, and as soon as we got out, we entered the hallway. So we couldn't see anything of our surroundings because we were covered by a tarpaulin, but we were still tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can I ask you: How long did you remain at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Batajnica for a total of 25 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me from Batajnica to Pale, by helicopter again, and that too was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you remember [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go to the period of time that you were in Batajnica, and I want to ask you about the conditions. But I'll ask you the questions, and then you can be focused on various aspects of the conditions in Batajnica and things that happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, before you do that, as a matter of clarification, I'm wondering, in terms of the indictment, count 1, re: persecutions, correct me if I'm wrong, but we seem to be restricted to persecutions throughout the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and elsewhere in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So I'm wondering what the relevance of what went on in or near Belgrade has. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, would Your Honour just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Firstly, it depicts a certain pattern in terms of persecutions, in the sense of two ethnic groups being targeted, perpetrators of a certain ethnic group, in other words, following the pattern that occurred in Odzak and Bosanski Samac. It also is relevant to the issue of systematic and widespread attack, because it shows the full scope and extent of the attack on those populations, not just in one geographical area but in another geographical area as well. And thirdly, it also demonstrates the international nature of the conflict, in other words, that people who are Bosnian, Bosnian citizens, were taken to Serbia and mistreated there. So that's the reason why it's relevant. I don't propose to go into this evidence chapter and verse in the same way that I dealt with the conditions in Bosanski Samac, of course. I propose to deal with it more speedily than I have with the other material. But they are the principal reasons why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What I just wanted to add on to what you were trying to explain was that, even though the indictment restricts the events, the occasions, to Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of former Yugoslavia, that's paragraph 6, maybe you are also trying to show that the atmosphere and the facilities, even in Belgrade or outside this territory described in the indictment, were also such that they were able to receive these people, and the torture and the ill-treated continued because it was directed against certain ethnic groups. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. That's one of the reasons, yes. Thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honour for putting it in that way, but that is one of the reasons as well why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Izetbegovic, perhaps you heard that exchange that I just had with the Judges, and I don't want to go into what happened at Batajnica in the same amount of detail that you have told us of events in Bosanski Samac, but I do want to know what happened there. Firstly, you've described in the past in your evidence that you were forced to stand and to sing Chetnik songs, or to sing Serbian songs. Did that occur at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of it occurred in Batajnica. It was the finale of the beatings. I apologise. I would like to tell you about Batajnica, for many reasons, because I still ask myself the question of why we had to go to another state with our own state [as interpreted]. Why didn't they take us to America or England or some other state? Why was it precisely to Yugoslavia, the then-Yugoslavia, when we were a sovereign and internationally recognised state ourselves? Why? And that is a very important point, and I want to have those details expounded, not only for me but with other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just leave that to us, Mr. Izetbegovic. But what I'm actually concerned with is conditions now in Batajnica, and I'm interested in the singing of songs and standing, standing up. Were you forced to stand up?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From 4.00 in the morning until the evening, we had, with brief intermissions for lunch, to stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any apparent reason why you were forced to stand?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason, as far as I was able to gather, except the desire to torture. My hands were swollen, as were the hands of others. We had to stand 30 centimetres from the wall, with our eyes bowed down, our hands beside our sides. Many of us couldn't take it. We would fall down from that rigidity. And if anybody did fall down, they would be beaten so hard that it's difficult to describe the intensity with which they would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of frequency this particular form of torture took, this standing, I mean. Was it a daily occurrence, a weekly occurrence in the time that you were there, every two or three days?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day. It happened daily. But as time went by, they would introduce new forms of torture. For example, they made me crawl through a small stool which was so narrow that I could hardly get my head through, but I'd have to crawl through without touching it. And when I didn't succeed in doing this, then they would beat me. And one of them said, "You'll lose enough weight to be able to crawl through that little stool in due course." And then they made us sing songs, and that's when the worst thing happened in the room next door to us. Other people were brought in. None of the rooms had doors. They were open apertures and you could hear all the conversations taking place. You could hear everything. Those people were brought in from somewhere around Bosanski Brod, the village of Kolibe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The question I asked you in relation to prisoners in Bosanski Samac was their ethnic background. What was the ethnic background of the prisoners in Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively and only Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber if the prisoners that you were incarcerated with at Batajnica appeared to you, for any reason, to be soldiers or ex-soldiers? Perhaps I should be clearer: captured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were young soldiers, regular soldiers, conscripts that were mobilised, and the reservists. In fact, it was all the Yugoslav army, and the uniforms were the same, that kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think perhaps you misunderstand me. I'm talking about the prisoners, the prisoners who were incarcerated with you, your fellow prisoners. Were they apparently captured soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. In the other room, when they brought those people from Bosanski Brod, one of them was wearing a camouflage uniform. They said he was an American. That's what people said, that he was an American mercenary. And there were two others, sort of partially dressed that way. One of them had military trousers and the other had a military shirt on. And then they would make us beat each other, and they would love this, this spectacle, and watch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let's just stop there and let's isolate each piece of activity so the Chamber can focus upon it. You've now mentioned being made to beat each other. What happened on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened was that when we beat each other, we tried to do this as painlessly as possible, but then they would notice that we weren't actually beating properly and then they'd take over. Then on one occasion they beat two people up really well and good. They gave them a good and proper beating. So there was no chance of beating less forcefully. And the worst thing was when they started to ill-treat us ourselves. They made this group of people perform oral sex on each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about that, but before I do so, can I ask you if you know -- if you know the names of any persons who were forced to engage in oral sex on each other, I'd ask you not to mention their actual names. Do you understand? So try and describe them in some other way. Now, tell us if you observed any sexual mistreatment of prisoners in the time that you were in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There were such things in the second group. Luckily, I myself did not experience this, but it was just a split second that prevented the same thing happening to us, us nine brought in from Posavina. But the other people did have to go through that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the second group. Which group is that? Are you referring to the group from Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the group from Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of sexual mistreatment did they suffer, and how do you know? How do you know that they suffered sexual mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were only separated by a part of the wall, everything else was open, open plan, and you could hear -- even with they were whispering, you could hear what was going on and the orders that had been given. And from the orders, we understood what he said. He said, "Form two lines. Take the bottom part off. Turn towards each other." And then he said quite clearly, "You're going to perform oral sex, first of all one kind and then the other kind -- one line, sorry, one line and then the other line." And that's what happened. And he would say, "This one's a professional. This one's an amateur." Then they'd start beating. It was terrible. And then somebody turned up. Somebody came and there was a melee of some kind, and we were spared having to go through that ugly act further. And allegedly -- and actually, the others never came back, those who made us do that, who ordered us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do I take it --

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do I take it from your last answer that this occasion was a once-off occasion of sexual misconduct? It wasn't repeated again?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I experienced it only once. I don't know what happened later on, whether anybody else came, because I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you just answer my next two questions with a yes or no. Were you beaten whilst you were at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very hard. More than in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see other people beaten?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the nine of us being beaten, whereas in the other room, when they joined us together with this other group and had to beat each other, one had his skull smashed in. And Dr. Kedacic examined him and said that he was a goner. And he screamed so much that it was terrible to hear. And he said, "I can't help him." And they made the doctor -- because they knew that he was a doctor, they made him do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you were personally being beaten, were any instruments used?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat us in Belgrade exclusively with batons and with their feet - they kicked us - and with their arms. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about the use of objects or instruments when other people, apart from yourself, were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in the next-door room they used this, when they managed to bash in the skull of this man, but in our own room, I didn't notice any other objects or instruments. Possibly there were some, but I didn't notice any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You keep referring to your own room. Do I take it that you were incarcerated for a longish period of time at Batajnica with the same group of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were nine of us. We were all together in one room all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Bosanski Samac people?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember some of them, some of their names, the nine of you who were together in the one room?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, Mr. Lukac, Mr. Barukcic, Mr. Sejo the policeman, [redacted] Mr. Dragicevic, Mr. Anto the vet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself. Is that nine?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's close enough. Thank you, Mr. Izetbegovic. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that you were in Batajnica, were you interrogated from time to time?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken out three times. They would come to fetch me, put handcuffs on me, tie my eyes and take me off somewhere. I assume that it was 3 or 4 kilometres away, because that's how long we spent in the vehicle. So I judged it to be that far away. Then I was led off by two people with my eyes blindfolded until they brought me to a room where they would interview me, interrogate me. Then they would take off my handcuffs, untie my blindfold, and I was able to see the room I was in and the people who were interviewing me. There were three of them or two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: During these occasions, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then. They did their work professionally. They were solicitous even. They gave me cigarettes, asked me if I was hungry. I suppose those are the methods they employ. They work that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of questions were you asked during these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me all kinds of things related to state authority, the party business, who I had contacted in Belgrade of the military authorities. I was somebody through whom an exchange had gone of Vukovar, and I know that -- the gentleman knew full well that I was the representative of the authorities from Bosanski Samac and I was in charge of civilian defence, civil defence for one period, and those were my obligations and responsibilities. Then there were people from the ministries of Bosnia. There was a police minister from Belgrade. And General Tomanov who came from Belgrade, who was head of Kos for Yugoslavia at the time. I knew him very well. Then there was General Puljic and many other important people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do I understand you that you were asked questions about these personalities?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood correctly. They asked me about those people, what I had to do with them. And I kept repeating, "Please, if you can, could you bring General Tomanov here? He knows about all my activities and my intentions, what they were, that I'm not to blame for anything." And I kept saying that if they put me in contact with him, that he would take me under his protection, that they would release me. But they didn't allow that to happen. And they asked me what I talked to him about when I had the meeting with the general. So that is that unfortunate UDBA organisation, and the police that never works the way it should. And on two occasions ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if on any occasion that -- during your period of time in Batajnica, or indeed in Bosanski Samac, when you were locked up, incarcerated, if you were ever told of any charge that had been brought against you, the nature of the charge, the nature of any wrong that you had committed.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that I was charged with having overthrown and taken part in the breakdown of the Yugoslav system. I don't remember what count. And I thought, What Yugoslavia? We're no longer in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are Bosnia-Herzegovina, a recognised state. It was nowhere in my mind to overthrow or break down something and to make it topple. I wouldn't have know how to go about anything like that anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When were you informed of the charge of having overthrown or taken part in the breakdown of the Yugoslav system; whilst at Batajnica or in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first processing took place in Bosanski Samac, and then in Batajnica, that was at the end, because a big file followed me there, and they had a big file on me in front of them there. And I heard about some things for the first time there. They told me who I was and what I was. I had no idea that I was that kind of person. And all that was the same was my name and surname. But they told me all these things and charged me with having overthrown the system, and what were my intentions in future. And they condemned me and read out my death sentence in front of a line-up. And they said that the execution would take place over the next few days when they read all this out, the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get to the death sentence in just a moment, but let's go back to the first processing in Bosanski Samac. I asked you when you were first informed about the charge of insurrection or overthrowing the Yugoslav system, and you said the first processing took place in Bosanski Samac. Do I take it from that answer that you meant that you were first informed of the charge in Bosanski Samac? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who informed you of the charge?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that by the person interviewing me, Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic, the interrogator.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, let's go back to Batajnica. You mentioned a death sentence, when you were lined up and told. Firstly, were you the only person to be informed on this occasion of a death sentence? In other words, were you the only person lined up?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine of us from Bosanski Samac were all lined up, and Mr. Tihic was told, "You are the lawyer. You were the public prosecutor. You are well-versed in reading out things of this kind." So he read it out to me. To all nine of us, actually. For us two there was this sentence. And he brought Belgrade newspapers where this had been published anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On this occasion when you were lined up and told that the death sentence had been passed upon you, were you informed what it was for? In other words, was there some connection between the imposition of this death sentence and overthrowing the system or whatever that you'd been informed about in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly based on everything from Bosanski Samac. And they kept talking about the undermining and overthrow of the system and the failure to report for the mobilisation of the army, that he hadn't responded to the call-up, that I was seen as a deserter. And I said, "Well, it's no longer my army. It was once, but it is no longer my army. It's a different country altogether, a different state altogether." That was my defence. I defended myself in that way. However, they did what they wanted to, and that's how everything ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You say they kept talking about the undermining and the overthrow of the system and the failure to report for the mobilisation of the army. Who kept talking on about that?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely those people who interrogated us throughout that time, Sarkanovic in Bosanski Samac and the ones in Belgrade, because they were the only ones that gave us reasons for which we were there. That was the reason they gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. That explains it. If you can answer my next question with a yes or no, please do. In the time that you were incarcerated in Bosanski Samac and Batajnica, did you ever have access to a lawyer or facilities to defend yourself against these charges?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing existed there that was anything similar to a civilised form of conduct. The lawyer was something you could only dream about. On one occasion in Belgrade, I asked for a physician, to see a doctor because I was in pain, I had a lot of pain. And they said, "You'll get a doctor." And then they came by in the evening and gave me an even greater beating. He said, "I'm the doctor and here you are." Heaven forbid, no lawyer of any kind, nor did anybody ever ask us. All we had to do was to keep quiet, to keep silent, and they would inform us, they would tell us. We didn't have the right to say anything. If we told the truth, we would be beaten. If we said what they liked to hear, well, they would accept it and support it and then give us a lecture back and brainwash us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In the time that you were at Batajnica, did [redacted] [redacted] Franjo Barukcic leave the prison or the cells?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where they separated them from us?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no. What I mean was were they actually permanently taken away from the prison at Batajnica or the place that you were detained at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken away first, so I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Tihic, Sulejman Tihic? Was he still there when you were taken away or had he been transferred somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I learnt was after the camp, Tihic was taken to Mitrovica the next day. One day after me, he was taken to Mitrovica. Some were returned. [redacted] others were taken back to Samac, but the others were taken away. I learnt that when we met up again after the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you've given evidence that you were transferred eventually from Batajnica. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was transferred to Pale, to General Mladic, and I had personal contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get there in due course, but first of all, can you remember the date on which you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was transferred on the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you transferred alone or did other prisoners go with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it a civilian helicopter or an army helicopter, air force helicopter?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Army helicopter, and there were 25 people armed to the teeth in it, soldiers, army soldiers belonging to the Yugoslav army who were going on assignment to Pale as reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Pale?

utterances.speaker: IZET IZETBEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at Pale -- before the helicopter started, let me just mention that an officer came up to me. He was a captain by rank, a young man. He was a captain in the Yugoslav army. You could see that he was something different than many of the others. He gave me some cigarettes. He said, "We don't know each other. I know what you have had to go through. I'm very sorry for that. I don't know where you're going." But he gave me a couple of boxes of cigarettes. He talked to me. He showed me some planes, the plane that had come from America or Canada, the one that Kikas, whom I was in the room with, had brought the weapons. He showed two airplanes of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said, "Those are the planes." And he was a very nice man, very frank, and his conduct was very proper. He said goodbye to me very nicely. He said, "See how you're going to fare." And that's it. We got to Pale, but on the way I was so frightened that they might throw me out, because from the very beginning they had masked their faces, were using different paints and colours, and they were prepared for an immediate assignment. And I think that's what happened as soon as we landed. We got out and we heard the people greeting them, saying, "Have you brought Izetbegovic?" And the person in charge of me said, "Yes, General." Now, which general it was, I don't know, but when I got out, General Mladic was standing there and he introduced himself, said, "I'm General Mladic." That was the first time that I had heard of him. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Now, if Your Honours please, I think you can tell that I'm nearing the end of my examination-in-chief, and I'll finish it -- it's now 1.00. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. With the leave of the Chamber, I suggest that we break, and I could finish this witness's testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because it's our lunch-hour break. And the question that Judge Williams raised about the indictment limiting the activities to the territory, and the point which I made, perhaps the Prosecution should look at this seriously concerning the whole indictment and the charges and see whether or not at this early stage it would be necessary to have an amendment. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's your case, so you decide. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
